link|Q11516023}} == Japanese content == {{Confused|Tsukiyomi-no-miya}} {{Shinto shrine |Image = [[File:Geku Tsukiyomi no Miya in October 2016.jpg|270px]]
Shrine buildings |Name = Tsukiyomi-no-miya |Location = Miyago 1-chome 3-19, {{jalink|Mie Prefecture|Q128196}}{{jalink|Ise City|Q328067}} |Coordinates = {{Coord|34|29|34.7|N|136|42|21.3|E|display=inline,title}} |Enshrined deity = {{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}}
Aramitama (rough spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto |Shrine rank = {{jalink|Shikinaisha}} (minor)
Betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of {{jalink|Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343}} |Founded = Before the 5th year of Engi (927) |Main sanctuary style = {{jalink|Shinmei-zukuri|Q930545}} |Annual festival = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Mie|lat_deg=34|lat_min=29|lat_sec=34.7|lon_deg=136|lon_min=42|lon_sec=21.3|label=Tsukiyomi-no-miya|position=top|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|marker=religious-shinto|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|34|29|34.7|N|136|42|21.3|E}}}} }} **Tsukiyomi-no-miya** (つきよみのみや) is a Shinto shrine in Miyago, {{jalink|Ise City|Q328067}}, {{jalink|Mie Prefecture|Q128196}}. It is a betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of the Outer Shrine (Gekū), {{jalink|Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343}}, of the {{jalink|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168}} complex.Tatsumi Publishing (2013): p. 16Ise Bunkasha, ed. (2008): p. 39Mirai Publishing (2013): p. 64Gakken Publishing (2013): p. 69JTB Publishing (2011): p. 42Publishing Business Headquarters, Domestic Information Dept., Third Editorial Dept., ed. (2014): p. 34Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 124 It is also a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}}. === Enshrined deities === {{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|**Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**}} (つきよみのみこと) **{{jalink|Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}}** (つきよみのみことのあらみたま) :Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto is the same deity as Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, who is enshrined at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine (Naikū). He is also said to be the younger brother of {{jalink|Amaterasu|Q455602}}. Because people historically planned farm work using a lunar calendar ({{jalink|lunar calendar|Q185688}}) based on the waxing and waning of the moon, he has been regarded as a deity connected with agriculture. He is also considered a river deity of Takagawara and a deity connected with women as well. In *Shinmei Hisho*, the sacred object ({{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}) is described as a {{jalink|mirror|Q35197}}. === Overview === [[File:Tsukiyomi-nomiya(Geku)_00.JPG|thumb|300px|right|Tsukiyomi-no-miya seen from above]] Tsukiyomi-no-miya is a betsugu of the Outer Shrine located about 300 m north of the Gekū and about 500 m west of {{jalink|Ise-shi Station|Q6079748}}. Two deities—{{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}} and his aramitama (rough/active spirit), **Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**—are enshrined together in the same shrine building. At Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and his aramitama are enshrined in separate buildings, but at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月夜見宮) they are enshrined together, which is a distinguishing feature. Other betsugu that enshrine two deities in a single building include {{jalink|Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463}} (an Outer Shrine betsugu) and {{jalink|Kaza-hi-no-miya|Q11665488}} (an Inner Shrine betsugu), both of which enshrine Shinatsuhiko-no-Mikoto and Shinatobe-no-Mikoto. Among the Outer Shrine’s betsugu, this is the only shrine located outside the main sacred precinct (miyagi). Although it stands in the urban area of Ise, the grounds retain a quiet atmosphere. The moat surrounding three sides of the precinct is thought to be a remnant of a tributary of the {{jalink|Miyagawa River (Mie)|Q6884164}}. {{jalink|Mie Prefectural Route 37 (Toba–Matsusaka Line)|Q11357923}}, which runs along the north side of the moat, becomes the venue for **{{jalink|Hatsuhiki|Q?}}** (the “Oise Grand Festival”) held each October in conjunction with the {{jalink|Kannamesai|Q11255045}}, and the ceremonial carts carrying first fruits into the Outer Shrine pass through. The Outer Shrine’s sessha (subsidiary shrine), **{{jalink|Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931}}**, is located behind the right side of the main shrine building. Behind the left side, an {{jalink|Inari}} is enshrined. To the right stands a large camphor tree, where some visitors offer prayers. As with other outlying betsugu, there is a **shukueiya** (a station where shrine staff stay during visiting hours), which distributes amulets and talismans and arranges kagura performances and offerings. === History === Its origins are not certain, but it is said that in ancient times it was called **Takagawara** and was a shrine that enshrined an agricultural deity. In the *Engishiki* compiled in 927 (the 5th year of Engi) during the reign of the 60th emperor, {{jalink|Emperor Daigo|Q329753}}, it was ranked first among the Outer Shrine’s sessha. In the *Toyuke-no-miya Gishikichō* it is recorded as “Tsukuyomi Shrine,” in the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō* as “Tsukiyomi Shrine,” and in the *Ise Daijingū Shiki* as “Tsukiyomi Sha.” In 1210 (the 4th year of Jōgen), it was elevated to the status of a betsugu.Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 125 In the Meiji period, the Outer Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月夜見宮**, while the Inner Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月讀宮**. During the {{jalink|Ise riot|Q11379085}} of 1876 (Meiji 9), nearby towns burned, and because of concern that the fire might spread to Tsukiyomi-no-miya, the sacred object ({{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}) was temporarily moved to {{jalink|Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463}}.Kaneko (1983): p. 214 During the {{jalink|Pacific War|Q184425}}, the {{jalink|Ujiyamada air raid|Q18990749}} occurred on July 29, 1945 (Shōwa 20). Although all surrounding houses burned down, due to desperate firefighting by the {{jalink|military|Q8473}} and the fact that an incendiary bomb lodged in the thatched roof failed to explode, only the shrine buildings of Tsukiyomi-no-miya remained standing amid the ruins.Yano (2006): pp. 184–185 However, a contracted shukueiin (guard attendant) was killed in the air raid, and the miyatsukasa (shrine official) suffered severe burns.Yano (2006): p. 185 === Festivals === Rites comparable to those of the Inner Shrine are performed, and for the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, Kannamesai, and Niinamesai, offerings ({{jalink|heihaku|Q11481885}}) are presented from the {{jalink|Imperial Household|Q909452}}. * January ** Saitansai (New Year’s Day Festival) (January 1) A festival celebrating the New Year and praying for the eternal continuity of the imperial line. ** Genshisai (January 3) A festival celebrating the origin of the imperial succession at the start of the year. * February ** Kenkoku Kinen-sai (National Foundation Festival) (February 11) A festival celebrating the founding of the nation by {{jalink|Emperor Jimmu|Q200188}}. ** Kinensai (February 18) A festival held at the beginning of the year praying for abundant harvests and national peace. ** Tenchōsai (February 23) A festival celebrating the birthday of {{jalink|Emperor Naruhito}}. * May ** Kazahinomisai (May 14) A rite in which offerings are presented not only at the Outer and Inner Shrines but also at betsugu, massha, and sessha, praying that there will be no damage from wind and rain and that the five grains will be abundant. * June ** Tsukinamisai (June 18–19) A festival held in June and December on the 11th, praying for national peace and the emperor’s well-being; at the Shrine it is also called one of the “Three Seasonal Festivals” together with the Kannamesai. * August ** Kazahinomisai (August 4) Same as above. * October ** {{jalink|Kannamesai|Q11255045}} (October 18–19) A festival in which priests offer newly harvested grain as sacred food ({{jalink|shinsen|Q11591045|Ōmike}}). * November ** {{jalink|Niinamesai|Q11501518}} (November 24) A festival in which the emperor offers newly harvested grain to the gods, partakes of it himself, and gives thanks for the harvest. * December ** Tsukinamisai (December 18–19) === Shikinen sengū === [[File:Sengu of Tsukiyomi no Miya, August 2014.jpg|thumb|Tsukiyomi-no-miya before the Ritchūsai (photo taken August 11, 2014)
Left: the then-current shrine building; right: the shrine building under construction]] The ceremonies and schedule for the 62nd shikinen sengū of Tsukiyomi-no-miya are as follows:{{Cite web|ja|url=http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|title=Another “moon deity” of Ise Grand Shrine’s Outer Shrine betsugu also moves—only Kaze-no-miya remains|publisher=Ise-Shima Keizai Shimbun|date=2015-03-03|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307142246/http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|archivedate=2015-03-07}}{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|title=Relocations of 12 betsugu including Tsukiyomi-no-miya - Ise Grand Shrine|publisher=Jingu Administration Office|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210061619/http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|archivedate=2015-02-10}} **2014** * August 20 – Ritchūsai (Pillar-Raising Festival) / Jōtōsai (Ridgepole-Raising Festival) * October 5 – Nokitsukesai (Eaves-Attaching Festival) * November 5 – Irakasai (Roofing Festival) **2015** * February 26 – Mitosai / Mifunashiro Hōnōshiki / Araikiyome * February 27 – Kotsukisai / Gochinsai / Kawara Ōharae * February 28 – Okazari / Sengyo (Transfer of the deity) * March 1 – Ōmike / Hōhei Among these, the Ritchūsai, Jōtōsai, Kotsukisai, Gochinsai, Sengyo, and Hōhei are conducted according to dates determined by imperial decision. In addition, on February 22, 2015, the **Oshiraishi-mochi** event was held, in which about 1,000 people of the Miyago offering group pulled ceremonial carts loaded with sacred white stones for 1.2 km from the Uraguchi intersection to Tsukiyomi-no-miya.{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|title=“Enya” linking to the next generation: Oshiraishi-mochi event at Tsukiyomi-no-miya in Ise|author=Yudai Nakahira|publisher=Chunichi Shimbun|date=2015-02-23|accessdate=2015-03-08|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307161058/http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|archivedate=2015-03-07}} With this, all oshiraishi-mochi events for the betsugu were completed. === Precincts === * Tsukiyomi-no-miya — A betsugu of the Outer Shrine (Gekū) of the Ise Grand Shrine complex. In keeping with the Outer Shrine, the thatched **shinmei-zukuri** building faces south and has outward-cut chigi and five (an odd number) katsuogi. The old site for relocation (kodenchi) lies adjacent to it east–west. As with the Outer Shrine, a relocation ({{jalink|Shikinen sengū|Q3959472}}) is performed once every 20 years. There is a tradition that when people of Miyago pulled the “yakukan” (construction timber) and reached Yōkaichiba-chō, a fire broke out in Miyago, and the pullers returned to fight it; the people of Yōkaichiba-chō took over pulling the timber, and ever since, at the **{{jalink|Okihiki-zome-shiki|Q11489125}}** the people of Yōkaichiba-chō have pulled and offered the timber to Tsukiyomi-no-miya. * {{jalink|Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931}} — Enshrined deity: the mitama (spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto. Located within the precincts of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, but it is a sessha of Toyouke Daijingu (the Outer Shrine) of Ise Grand Shrine. * {{jalink|Inari Shrine}} * Shukueiya === Kamiji Street === [[File:Kamiji Street from Tsukiyomi no Miya.jpg|thumb|Kamiji Street]] The straight road about 4 m wide running from the Outer Shrine’s Kita-mikado (North Gate) to Tsukiyomi-no-miya is regarded as “the road the gods pass,” and is called **Kamiji Street** (神路通り). See the article {{jalink|Kamiji Street|Q30114580}}. === Devotee organization === In 1960 (Shōwa 35), a Tsukiyomi confraternity (Tsukiyomi-kō) was formed mainly by worshippers living in Ise, later renamed the Tsukiyomi-no-miya Hōsankai. The Hōsankai carries out activities such as holding a festival of gratitude for divine blessings on April 19 and September 19 each year. === Access === * About a 10-minute walk from {{jalink|Ise-shi Station|Q6079748}} on the JR {{jalink|Sangū Line|Q872023}} and the Kintetsu Yamada Line. * About a 5-minute walk from the Outer Shrine Kita-mikado entrance via {{jalink|Kamiji Street|Q30114580}}.JTB Publishing (2011): p. 43 * About a 3-minute walk from the Shindō bus stop (Mie Kōtsū), and immediately from the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop on the Ise City community bus “Okage Bus.”From July 20, 2013, Mie Kōtsū’s “Sangū Bus” stopped at the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop, but as of March 31, 2015, service to that stop was discontinued. * About 3 km from the Ise Interchange on the {{jalink|Ise Expressway|Q6079578}}. * Parking: Only 2–4 cars can park in front of the torii gate, but there are parking meters on the road to the south. === Notes === {{Reflist|2}} === References === * *A Guide to Visiting Tsukiyomi-no-miya* (published by the Jingu Administration Office) * *Let’s Walk Around Oise-san* (published by the Ise Jingu Sūkeikai) * *Oise Mairi* (published by the Ise Jingu Sūkeikai) * Publications, Aug. 30, 2013, 230 pp. ISBN 978-4-02-273516-4 * Kenichi Yano, *Ise Jingu—Inside the Unfamiliar Sacred Grove*, Kadokawa Sensho 402, Kadokawa Gakugei Shuppan, Nov. 10, 2006, 270 pp. ISBN 4-04-703402-9 * *Ise Jingu*, Rakugaku Books: Shrines 1, JTB Publishing, Apr. 1, 2011, 143 pp. ISBN 978-4-533-08206-1 * *If You’re Japanese, You Should Know: Ise Jingu and 125 Shrines*, Tatsumi Mook, It is a betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of the Outer Shrine (Gekū), {{jalink|Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343}}, of the {{jalink|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168}} complex.Tatsumi Publishing (2013): p. 16Ise Bunkasha, ed. (2008): p. 39Mirai Publishing (2013): p. 64Gakken Publishing (2013): p. 69JTB Publishing (2011): p. 42Publishing Business Headquarters, Domestic Information Dept., Third Editorial Dept., ed. (2014): p. 34Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 124 It is also a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}}. === Enshrined deities === {{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|**Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**}} (つきよみのみこと) **{{jalink|Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}}** (つきよみのみことのあらみたま) :Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto is the same deity as Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, who is enshrined at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine (Naikū). He is also said to be the younger brother of {{jalink|Amaterasu|Q455602}}. Because people historically planned farm work using a lunar calendar ({{jalink|lunar calendar|Q185688}}) based on the waxing and waning of the moon, he has been regarded as a deity connected with agriculture. He is also considered a river deity of Takagawara and a deity connected with women as well. In *Shinmei Hisho*, the sacred object ({{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}) is described as a {{jalink|mirror|Q35197}}. === Overview === [[File:Tsukiyomi-nomiya(Geku)_00.JPG|thumb|300px|right|Tsukiyomi-no-miya seen from above]] Tsukiyomi-no-miya is a betsugu of the Outer Shrine located about 300 m north of the Gekū and about 500 m west of {{jalink|Ise-shi Station|Q6079748}}. Two deities—{{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}} and his aramitama (rough/active spirit), **Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**—are enshrined together in the same shrine building. At Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and his aramitama are enshrined in separate buildings, but at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月夜見宮) they are enshrined together, which is a distinguishing feature. Other betsugu that enshrine two deities in a single building include {{jalink|Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463}} (an Outer Shrine betsugu) and {{jalink|Kaza-hi-no-miya|Q11665488}} (an Inner Shrine betsugu), both of which enshrine Shinatsuhiko-no-Mikoto and Shinatobe-no-Mikoto. Among the Outer Shrine’s betsugu, this is the only shrine located outside the main sacred precinct (miyagi). Although it stands in the urban area of Ise, the grounds retain a quiet atmosphere. The moat surrounding three sides of the precinct is thought to be a remnant of a tributary of the {{jalink|Miyagawa River (Mie)|Q6884164}}. {{jalink|Mie Prefectural Route 37 (Toba–Matsusaka Line)|Q11357923}}, which runs along the north side of the moat, becomes the venue for **{{jalink|Hatsuhiki|Q?}}** (the “Oise Grand Festival”) held each October in conjunction with the {{jalink|Kannamesai|Q11255045}}, and the ceremonial carts carrying first fruits into the Outer Shrine pass through. The Outer Shrine’s sessha (subsidiary shrine), **{{jalink|Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931}}**, is located behind the right side of the main shrine building. Behind the left side, an {{jalink|Inari}} is enshrined. To the right stands a large camphor tree, where some visitors offer prayers. As with other outlying betsugu, there is a **shukueiya** (a station where shrine staff stay during visiting hours), which distributes amulets and talismans and arranges kagura performances and offerings. === History === Its origins are not certain, but it is said that in ancient times it was called **Takagawara** and was a shrine that enshrined an agricultural deity. In the *Engishiki* compiled in 927 (the 5th year of Engi) during the reign of the 60th emperor, {{jalink|Emperor Daigo|Q329753}}, it was ranked first among the Outer Shrine’s sessha. In the *Toyuke-no-miya Gishikichō* it is recorded as “Tsukuyomi Shrine,” in the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō* as “Tsukiyomi Shrine,” and in the *Ise Daijingū Shiki* as “Tsukiyomi Sha.” In 1210 (the 4th year of Jōgen), it was elevated to the status of a betsugu.Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 125 In the Meiji period, the Outer Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月夜見宮**, while the Inner Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月讀宮**. During the {{jalink|Ise riot|Q11379085}} of 1876 (Meiji 9), nearby towns burned, and because of concern that the fire might spread to Tsukiyomi-no-miya, the sacred object ({{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}) was temporarily moved to {{jalink|Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463}}.Kaneko (1983): p. 214 During the {{jalink|Pacific War|Q184425}}, the {{jalink|Ujiyamada air raid|Q18990749}} occurred on July 29, 1945 (Shōwa 20). Although all surrounding houses burned down, due to desperate firefighting by the {{jalink|military|Q8473}} and the fact that an incendiary bomb lodged in the thatched roof failed to explode, only the shrine buildings of Tsukiyomi-no-miya remained standing amid the ruins.Yano (2006): pp. 184–185 However, a contracted shukueiin (guard attendant) was killed in the air raid, and the miyatsukasa (shrine official) suffered severe burns.Yano (2006): p. 185 === Festivals === Rites comparable to those of the Inner Shrine are performed, and for the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, Kannamesai, and Niinamesai, offerings ({{jalink|heihaku|Q11481885}}) are presented from the {{jalink|Imperial Household|Q909452}}. * January ** Saitansai (New Year’s Day Festival) (January 1) A festival celebrating the New Year and praying for the eternal continuity of the imperial line. ** Genshisai (January 3) A festival celebrating the origin of the imperial succession at the start of the year. * February ** Kenkoku Kinen-sai (National Foundation Festival) (February 11) A festival celebrating the founding of the nation by {{jalink|Emperor Jimmu|Q200188}}. ** Kinensai (February 18) A festival held at the beginning of the year praying for abundant harvests and national peace. ** Tenchōsai (February 23) A festival celebrating the birthday of {{jalink|Emperor Naruhito}}. * May ** Kazahinomisai (May 14) A rite in which offerings are presented not only at the Outer and Inner Shrines but also at betsugu, massha, and sessha, praying that there will be no damage from wind and rain and that the five grains will be abundant. * June ** Tsukinamisai (June 18–19) A festival held in June and December on the 11th, praying for national peace and the emperor’s well-being; at the Shrine it is also called one of the “Three Seasonal Festivals” together with the Kannamesai. * August ** Kazahinomisai (August 4) Same as above. * October ** {{jalink|Kannamesai|Q11255045}} (October 18–19) A festival in which priests offer newly harvested grain as sacred food ({{jalink|shinsen|Q11591045|Ōmike}}). * November ** {{jalink|Niinamesai|Q11501518}} (November 24) A festival in which the emperor offers newly harvested grain to the gods, partakes of it himself, and gives thanks for the harvest. * December ** Tsukinamisai (December 18–19) === Shikinen sengū === [[File:Sengu of Tsukiyomi no Miya, August 2014.jpg|thumb|Tsukiyomi-no-miya before the Ritchūsai (photo taken August 11, 2014)
Left: the then-current shrine building; right: the shrine building under construction]] The ceremonies and schedule for the 62nd shikinen sengū of Tsukiyomi-no-miya are as follows:{{Cite web|ja|url=http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|title=Another “moon deity” of Ise Grand Shrine’s Outer Shrine betsugu also moves—only Kaze-no-miya remains|publisher=Ise-Shima Keizai Shimbun|date=2015-03-03|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307142246/http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|archivedate=2015-03-07}}{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|title=Relocations of 12 betsugu including Tsukiyomi-no-miya - Ise Grand Shrine|publisher=Jingu Administration Office|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210061619/http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|archivedate=2015-02-10}} **2014** * August 20 – Ritchūsai (Pillar-Raising Festival) / Jōtōsai (Ridgepole-Raising Festival) * October 5 – Nokitsukesai (Eaves-Attaching Festival) * November 5 – Irakasai (Roofing Festival) **2015** * February 26 – Mitosai / Mifunashiro Hōnōshiki / Araikiyome * February 27 – Kotsukisai / Gochinsai / Kawara Ōharae * February 28 – Okazari / Sengyo (Transfer of the deity) * March 1 – Ōmike / Hōhei Among these, the Ritchūsai, Jōtōsai, Kotsukisai, Gochinsai, Sengyo, and Hōhei are conducted according to dates determined by imperial decision. In addition, on February 22, 2015, the **Oshiraishi-mochi** event was held, in which about 1,000 people of the Miyago offering group pulled ceremonial carts loaded with sacred white stones for 1.2 km from the Uraguchi intersection to Tsukiyomi-no-miya.{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|title=“Enya” linking to the next generation: Oshiraishi-mochi event at Tsukiyomi-no-miya in Ise|author=Yudai Nakahira|publisher=Chunichi Shimbun|date=2015-02-23|accessdate=2015-03-08|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307161058/http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|archivedate=2015-03-07}} With this, all oshiraishi-mochi events for the betsugu were completed. === Precincts === * Tsukiyomi-no-miya — A betsugu of the Outer Shrine (Gekū) of the Ise Grand Shrine complex. In keeping with the Outer Shrine, the thatched **shinmei-zukuri** building faces south and has outward-cut chigi and five (an odd number) katsuogi. The old site for relocation (kodenchi) lies adjacent to it east–west. As with the Outer Shrine, a relocation ({{jalink|Shikinen sengū|Q3959472}}) is performed once every 20 years. There is a tradition that when people of Miyago pulled the “yakukan” (construction timber) and reached Yōkaichiba-chō, a fire broke out in Miyago, and the pullers returned to fight it; the people of Yōkaichiba-chō took over pulling the timber, and ever since, at the **{{jalink|Okihiki-zome-shiki|Q11489125}}** the people of Yōkaichiba-chō have pulled and offered the timber to Tsukiyomi-no-miya. * {{jalink|Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931}} — Enshrined deity: the mitama (spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto. Located within the precincts of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, but it is a sessha of Toyouke Daijingu (the Outer Shrine) of Ise Grand Shrine. * {{jalink|Inari Shrine}} * Shukueiya === Kamiji Street === [[File:Kamiji Street from Tsukiyomi no Miya.jpg|thumb|Kamiji Street]] The straight road about 4 m wide running from the Outer Shrine’s Kita-mikado (North Gate) to Tsukiyomi-no-miya is regarded as “the road the gods pass,” and is called **Kamiji Street** (神路通り). See the article {{jalink|Kamiji Street|Q30114580}}. === Devotee organization === In 1960 (Shōwa 35), a Tsukiyomi confraternity (Tsukiyomi-kō) was formed mainly by worshippers living in Ise, later renamed the Tsukiyomi-no-miya Hōsankai. The Hōsankai carries out activities such as holding a festival of gratitude for divine blessings on April 19 and September 19 each year. === Access === * About a 10-minute walk from {{jalink|Ise-shi Station|Q6079748}} on the JR {{jalink|Sangū Line|Q872023}} and the Kintetsu Yamada Line. * About a 5-minute walk from the Outer Shrine Kita-mikado entrance via {{jalink|Kamiji Street|Q30114580}}.JTB Publishing (2011): p. 43 * About a 3-minute walk from the Shindō bus stop (Mie Kōtsū), and immediately from the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop on the Ise City community bus “Okage Bus.”From July 20, 2013, Mie Kōtsū’s “Sangū Bus” stopped at the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop, but as of March 31, 2015, service to that stop was discontinued. * About 3 km from the Ise Interchange on the {{jalink|Ise Expressway|Q6079578}}. * Parking: Only 2–4 cars can park in front of the torii gate, but there are parking meters on the road to the south. === Notes === {{Reflist|2}} === References === * *A Guide to Visiting Tsukiyomi-no-miya* (published by the Jingu Administration Office) * *Let’s Walk Around Oise-san* (published by the Ise Jingu Sūkeikai) * *Oise Mairi* (published by the Ise Jingu Sūkeikai) * *Ujiyamada City History* * Nobuo Kaneko, *Tamaki Town History, Vol. 2—History and Traditions of Southern Ise*, Mie Prefecture Local Materials Series No. 91, Mie Prefecture Local Materials Publication Publications, Aug. 30, 2013, 230 pp. ISBN 978-4-02-273516-4 * Kenichi Yano, *Ise Jingu—Inside the Unfamiliar Sacred Grove*, Kadokawa Sensho 402, Kadokawa Gakugei Shuppan, Nov. 10, 2006, 270 pp. ISBN Ise Jingu Pilgrimage Perfect Book*, Mirai Publishing, Dec. 10, 2013, 107 pp. ISBN 978-4-907292-14-0 === See also === * {{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520}} * {{jalink|List of Shikinaisha in Ise Province|Q11378973}} * {{jalink|List of 125 shrines of Jingu|Q16482760}} * {{jalink|Kamiji Street|Q30114580}} === External links === {{commonscat|Tsukiyomi-no-miya (Geku)}} * {{Wayback|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/about/geku/tsukiyomi.html |title=Tsukiyomi-no-miya |date=20170602200335}} - Official Ise Grand Shrine website * [http://www.jingukaikan.jp/125mairi/m02/0202.html Tsukiyomi-no-miya (つきよみのみや) - Jingu Kaikan] - Ise Jingu Sūkeikai (General Incorporated Foundation) * [http://www.ise-kanko.jp/base_data/base_data.php?info_cd=00269 Ise City Tourism Association / Tsukiyomi-no-miya] * [http://www.barifuri.com/tourcenter/data_kankou/tsukiyomi_1/index.html Tsukiyomi-no-miya (つきよみのみや)] - Ise-Shima Barrier-Free Tour Center {{Jingu 125 Shrines}} {{Shinto}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Tsukiyomi-no-miya}} == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Tsukiyomi-no-Miya (Geku)]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Tsukiyomi-no-Miya (Geku)]][[Category:Pages]] [[Category:Shikinai Shōsha]] [[Category:Shikinai Hiteisha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Ise Province]] [[Category:pages]] [[Category:神宮125社]] [[Category:伊勢国の式内社]] [[Category:伊勢市の神社]] [[Category:2015年竣工の日本の建築物]]

Shrine buildings |Name = Tsukiyomi-no-miya |Location = Miyago 1-chome 3-19, {{jalink|Mie Prefecture|Q128196}}{{jalink|Ise City|Q328067}} |Coordinates = {{Coord|34|29|34.7|N|136|42|21.3|E|display=inline,title}} |Enshrined deity = {{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}}
Aramitama (rough spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto |Shrine rank = {{jalink|Shikinaisha}} (minor)
Betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of {{jalink|Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343}} |Founded = Before the 5th year of Engi (927) |Main sanctuary style = {{jalink|Shinmei-zukuri|Q930545}} |Annual festival = |Map = {{Location map|Japan Mie|lat_deg=34|lat_min=29|lat_sec=34.7|lon_deg=136|lon_min=42|lon_sec=21.3|label=Tsukiyomi-no-miya|position=top|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|marker=religious-shinto|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|34|29|34.7|N|136|42|21.3|E}}}} }} **Tsukiyomi-no-miya** (つきよみのみや) is a Shinto shrine in Miyago, {{jalink|Ise City|Q328067}}, {{jalink|Mie Prefecture|Q128196}}. It is a betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of the Outer Shrine (Gekū), {{jalink|Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343}}, of the {{jalink|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168}} complex.Tatsumi Publishing (2013): p. 16Ise Bunkasha, ed. (2008): p. 39Mirai Publishing (2013): p. 64Gakken Publishing (2013): p. 69JTB Publishing (2011): p. 42Publishing Business Headquarters, Domestic Information Dept., Third Editorial Dept., ed. (2014): p. 34Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 124 It is also a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}}. === Enshrined deities === {{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|**Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**}} (つきよみのみこと) **{{jalink|Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}}** (つきよみのみことのあらみたま) :Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto is the same deity as Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, who is enshrined at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine (Naikū). He is also said to be the younger brother of {{jalink|Amaterasu|Q455602}}. Because people historically planned farm work using a lunar calendar ({{jalink|lunar calendar|Q185688}}) based on the waxing and waning of the moon, he has been regarded as a deity connected with agriculture. He is also considered a river deity of Takagawara and a deity connected with women as well. In *Shinmei Hisho*, the sacred object ({{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}) is described as a {{jalink|mirror|Q35197}}. === Overview === [[File:Tsukiyomi-nomiya(Geku)_00.JPG|thumb|300px|right|Tsukiyomi-no-miya seen from above]] Tsukiyomi-no-miya is a betsugu of the Outer Shrine located about 300 m north of the Gekū and about 500 m west of {{jalink|Ise-shi Station|Q6079748}}. Two deities—{{jalink|Tsukuyomi|Q595520|Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}} and his aramitama (rough/active spirit), **Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**—are enshrined together in the same shrine building. At Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and his aramitama are enshrined in separate buildings, but at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月夜見宮) they are enshrined together, which is a distinguishing feature. Other betsugu that enshrine two deities in a single building include {{jalink|Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463}} (an Outer Shrine betsugu) and {{jalink|Kaza-hi-no-miya|Q11665488}} (an Inner Shrine betsugu), both of which enshrine Shinatsuhiko-no-Mikoto and Shinatobe-no-Mikoto. Among the Outer Shrine’s betsugu, this is the only shrine located outside the main sacred precinct (miyagi). Although it stands in the urban area of Ise, the grounds retain a quiet atmosphere. The moat surrounding three sides of the precinct is thought to be a remnant of a tributary of the {{jalink|Miyagawa River (Mie)|Q6884164}}. {{jalink|Mie Prefectural Route 37 (Toba–Matsusaka Line)|Q11357923}}, which runs along the north side of the moat, becomes the venue for **{{jalink|Hatsuhiki|Q?}}** (the “Oise Grand Festival”) held each October in conjunction with the {{jalink|Kannamesai|Q11255045}}, and the ceremonial carts carrying first fruits into the Outer Shrine pass through. The Outer Shrine’s sessha (subsidiary shrine), **{{jalink|Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931}}**, is located behind the right side of the main shrine building. Behind the left side, an {{jalink|Inari}} is enshrined. To the right stands a large camphor tree, where some visitors offer prayers. As with other outlying betsugu, there is a **shukueiya** (a station where shrine staff stay during visiting hours), which distributes amulets and talismans and arranges kagura performances and offerings. === History === Its origins are not certain, but it is said that in ancient times it was called **Takagawara** and was a shrine that enshrined an agricultural deity. In the *Engishiki* compiled in 927 (the 5th year of Engi) during the reign of the 60th emperor, {{jalink|Emperor Daigo|Q329753}}, it was ranked first among the Outer Shrine’s sessha. In the *Toyuke-no-miya Gishikichō* it is recorded as “Tsukuyomi Shrine,” in the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō* as “Tsukiyomi Shrine,” and in the *Ise Daijingū Shiki* as “Tsukiyomi Sha.” In 1210 (the 4th year of Jōgen), it was elevated to the status of a betsugu.Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 125 In the Meiji period, the Outer Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月夜見宮**, while the Inner Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月讀宮**. During the {{jalink|Ise riot|Q11379085}} of 1876 (Meiji 9), nearby towns burned, and because of concern that the fire might spread to Tsukiyomi-no-miya, the sacred object ({{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}) was temporarily moved to {{jalink|Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463}}.Kaneko (1983): p. 214 During the {{jalink|Pacific War|Q184425}}, the {{jalink|Ujiyamada air raid|Q18990749}} occurred on July 29, 1945 (Shōwa 20). Although all surrounding houses burned down, due to desperate firefighting by the {{jalink|military|Q8473}} and the fact that an incendiary bomb lodged in the thatched roof failed to explode, only the shrine buildings of Tsukiyomi-no-miya remained standing amid the ruins.Yano (2006): pp. 184–185 However, a contracted shukueiin (guard attendant) was killed in the air raid, and the miyatsukasa (shrine official) suffered severe burns.Yano (2006): p. 185 === Festivals === Rites comparable to those of the Inner Shrine are performed, and for the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, Kannamesai, and Niinamesai, offerings ({{jalink|heihaku|Q11481885}}) are presented from the {{jalink|Imperial Household|Q909452}}. * January ** Saitansai (New Year’s Day Festival) (January 1) A festival celebrating the New Year and praying for the eternal continuity of the imperial line. ** Genshisai (January 3) A festival celebrating the origin of the imperial succession at the start of the year. * February ** Kenkoku Kinen-sai (National Foundation Festival) (February 11) A festival celebrating the founding of the nation by {{jalink|Emperor Jimmu|Q200188}}. ** Kinensai (February 18) A festival held at the beginning of the year praying for abundant harvests and national peace. ** Tenchōsai (February 23) A festival celebrating the birthday of {{jalink|Emperor Naruhito}}. * May ** Kazahinomisai (May 14) A rite in which offerings are presented not only at the Outer and Inner Shrines but also at betsugu, massha, and sessha, praying that there will be no damage from wind and rain and that the five grains will be abundant. * June ** Tsukinamisai (June 18–19) A festival held in June and December on the 11th, praying for national peace and the emperor’s well-being; at the Shrine it is also called one of the “Three Seasonal Festivals” together with the Kannamesai. * August ** Kazahinomisai (August 4) Same as above. * October ** {{jalink|Kannamesai|Q11255045}} (October 18–19) A festival in which priests offer newly harvested grain as sacred food ({{jalink|shinsen|Q11591045|Ōmike}}). * November ** {{jalink|Niinamesai|Q11501518}} (November 24) A festival in which the emperor offers newly harvested grain to the gods, partakes of it himself, and gives thanks for the harvest. * December ** Tsukinamisai (December 18–19) === Shikinen sengū === [[File:Sengu of Tsukiyomi no Miya, August 2014.jpg|thumb|Tsukiyomi-no-miya before the Ritchūsai (photo taken August 11, 2014)
Left: the then-current shrine building; right: the shrine building under construction]] The ceremonies and schedule for the 62nd shikinen sengū of Tsukiyomi-no-miya are as follows:{{Cite web|ja|url=http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|title=Another “moon deity” of Ise Grand Shrine’s Outer Shrine betsugu also moves—only Kaze-no-miya remains|publisher=Ise-Shima Keizai Shimbun|date=2015-03-03|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307142246/http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|archivedate=2015-03-07}}{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|title=Relocations of 12 betsugu including Tsukiyomi-no-miya - Ise Grand Shrine|publisher=Jingu Administration Office|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210061619/http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|archivedate=2015-02-10}} **2014** * August 20 – Ritchūsai (Pillar-Raising Festival) / Jōtōsai (Ridgepole-Raising Festival) * October 5 – Nokitsukesai (Eaves-Attaching Festival) * November 5 – Irakasai (Roofing Festival) **2015** * February 26 – Mitosai / Mifunashiro Hōnōshiki / Araikiyome * February 27 – Kotsukisai / Gochinsai / Kawara Ōharae * February 28 – Okazari / Sengyo (Transfer of the deity) * March 1 – Ōmike / Hōhei Among these, the Ritchūsai, Jōtōsai, Kotsukisai, Gochinsai, Sengyo, and Hōhei are conducted according to dates determined by imperial decision. In addition, on February 22, 2015, the **Oshiraishi-mochi** event was held, in which about 1,000 people of the Miyago offering group pulled ceremonial carts loaded with sacred white stones for 1.2 km from the Uraguchi intersection to Tsukiyomi-no-miya.{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|title=“Enya” linking to the next generation: Oshiraishi-mochi event at Tsukiyomi-no-miya in Ise|author=Yudai Nakahira|publisher=Chunichi Shimbun|date=2015-02-23|accessdate=2015-03-08|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307161058/http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|archivedate=2015-03-07}} With this, all oshiraishi-mochi events for the betsugu were completed. === Precincts === * Tsukiyomi-no-miya — A betsugu of the Outer Shrine (Gekū) of the Ise Grand Shrine complex. In keeping with the Outer Shrine, the thatched **shinmei-zukuri** building faces south and has outward-cut chigi and five (an odd number) katsuogi. The old site for relocation (kodenchi) lies adjacent to it east–west. As with the Outer Shrine, a relocation ({{jalink|Shikinen sengū|Q3959472}}) is performed once every 20 years. There is a tradition that when people of Miyago pulled the “yakukan” (construction timber) and reached Yōkaichiba-chō, a fire broke out in Miyago, and the pullers returned to fight it; the people of Yōkaichiba-chō took over pulling the timber, and ever since, at the **{{jalink|Okihiki-zome-shiki|Q11489125}}** the people of Yōkaichiba-chō have pulled and offered the timber to Tsukiyomi-no-miya. * {{jalink|Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931}} — Enshrined deity: the mitama (spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto. Located within the precincts of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, but it is a sessha of Toyouke Daijingu (the Outer Shrine) of Ise Grand Shrine. * {{jalink|Inari Shrine}} * Shukueiya === Kamiji Street === [[File:Kamiji Street from Tsukiyomi no Miya.jpg|thumb|Kamiji Street]] The straight road about 4 m wide running from the Outer Shrine’s Kita-mikado (North Gate) to Tsukiyomi-no-miya is regarded as “the road the gods pass,” and is called **Kamiji Street** (神路通り). See the article {{jalink|Kamiji Street|Q30114580}}. === Devotee organization === In 1960 (Shōwa 35), a Tsukiyomi confraternity (Tsukiyomi-kō) was formed mainly by worshippers living in Ise, later renamed the Tsukiyomi-no-miya Hōsankai. The Hōsankai carries out activities such as holding a festival of gratitude for divine blessings on April 19 and September 19 each year. === Access === * About a 10-minute walk from {{jalink|Ise-shi Station|Q6079748}} on the JR {{jalink|Sangū Line|Q872023}} and the Kintetsu Yamada Line. * About a 5-minute walk from the Outer Shrine Kita-mikado entrance via {{jalink|Kamiji Street|Q30114580}}.JTB Publishing (2011): p. 43 * About a 3-minute walk from the Shindō bus stop (Mie Kōtsū), and immediately from the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop on the Ise City community bus “Okage Bus.”From July 20, 2013, Mie Kōtsū’s “Sangū Bus” stopped at the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop, but as of March 31, 2015, service to that stop was discontinued. * About 3 km from the Ise Interchange on the {{jalink|Ise Expressway|Q6079578}}. * Parking: Only 2–4 cars can park in front of the torii gate, but there are parking meters on the road to the south. === Notes === {{Reflist|2}} === References === * *A Guide to Publications, Aug. 30, 2013, 230 pp. ISBN 978-4-02-273516-4 * Kenichi Yano, *Ise Jingu—Inside the Unfamiliar Sacred Grove*, Kadokawa Sensho 402, Kadokawa Gakugei Shuppan, Nov. 10, 2006, 270 pp. ISBN It is a betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of the Outer Shrine (Gekū), {{ill|lt=Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343|WD=Q11633343}}, of the {{ill|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168|WD=Q687168}} complex.Tatsumi Publishing (2013): p. 16Ise Bunkasha, ed. (2008): p. 39Mirai Publishing (2013): p. 64Gakken Publishing (2013): p. 69JTB Publishing (2011): p. 42Publishing Business Headquarters, Domestic Information Dept., Third Editorial Dept., ed. (2014): p. 34Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 124 It is also a {{ill||lt=Shikinaisha|UNKNOWN}}. === Enshrined deities === {{ill|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520|lt=**Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**}} (つきよみのみこと) **{{ill||lt=Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto|UNKNOWN}}** (つきよみのみことのあらみたま) :Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto is the same deity as Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, who is enshrined at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine (Naikū). He is also said to be the younger brother of {{ill|lt=Amaterasu|Q455602|WD=Q455602}}. Because people historically planned farm work using a lunar calendar ({{ill|lt=lunar calendar|Q185688|WD=Q185688}}) based on the waxing and waning of the moon, he has been regarded as a deity connected with agriculture. He is also considered a river deity of Takagawara and a deity connected with women as well. In *Shinmei Hisho*, the sacred object ({{ill|lt=shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532}}) is described as a {{ill|lt=mirror|Q35197|WD=Q35197}}. === Overview === [[File:Tsukiyomi-nomiya(Geku)_00.JPG|thumb|300px|right|Tsukiyomi-no-miya seen from above]] Tsukiyomi-no-miya is a betsugu of the Outer Shrine located about 300 m north of the Gekū and about 500 m west of {{ill|lt=Ise-shi Station|Q6079748|WD=Q6079748}}. Two deities—{{ill|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520|lt=Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}} and his aramitama (rough/active spirit), **Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**—are enshrined together in the same shrine building. At Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and his aramitama are enshrined in separate buildings, but at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月夜見宮) they are enshrined together, which is a distinguishing feature. Other betsugu that enshrine two deities in a single building include {{ill|lt=Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463|WD=Q11665463}} (an Outer Shrine betsugu) and {{ill|lt=Kaza-hi-no-miya|Q11665488|WD=Q11665488}} (an Inner Shrine betsugu), both of which enshrine Shinatsuhiko-no-Mikoto and Shinatobe-no-Mikoto. Among the Outer Shrine’s betsugu, this is the only shrine located outside the main sacred precinct (miyagi). Although it stands in the urban area of Ise, the grounds retain a quiet atmosphere. The moat surrounding three sides of the precinct is thought to be a remnant of a tributary of the {{ill|lt=Miyagawa River (Mie)|Q6884164|WD=Q6884164}}. {{ill|lt=Mie Prefectural Route 37 (Toba–Matsusaka Line)|Q11357923|WD=Q11357923}}, which runs along the north side of the moat, becomes the venue for **{{ill||lt=Hatsuhiki|UNKNOWN}}** (the “Oise Grand Festival”) held each October in conjunction with the {{ill|lt=Kannamesai|Q11255045|WD=Q11255045}}, and the ceremonial carts carrying first fruits into the Outer Shrine pass through. The Outer Shrine’s sessha (subsidiary shrine), **{{ill|lt=Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931|WD=Q17225931}}**, is located behind the right side of the main shrine building. Behind the left side, an {{ill||lt=Inari|UNKNOWN}} is enshrined. To the right stands a large camphor tree, where some visitors offer prayers. As with other outlying betsugu, there is a **shukueiya** (a station where shrine staff stay during visiting hours), which distributes amulets and talismans and arranges kagura performances and offerings. === History === Its origins are not certain, but it is said that in ancient times it was called **Takagawara** and was a shrine that enshrined an agricultural deity. In the *Engishiki* compiled in 927 (the 5th year of Engi) during the reign of the 60th emperor, {{ill|lt=Emperor Daigo|Q329753|WD=Q329753}}, it was ranked first among the Outer Shrine’s sessha. In the *Toyuke-no-miya Gishikichō* it is recorded as “Tsukuyomi Shrine,” in the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō* as “Tsukiyomi Shrine,” and in the *Ise Daijingū Shiki* as “Tsukiyomi Sha.” In 1210 (the 4th year of Jōgen), it was elevated to the status of a betsugu.Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 125 In the Meiji period, the Outer Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月夜見宮**, while the Inner Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月讀宮**. During the {{ill|lt=Ise riot|Q11379085|WD=Q11379085}} of 1876 (Meiji 9), nearby towns burned, and because of concern that the fire might spread to Tsukiyomi-no-miya, the sacred object ({{ill|lt=shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532}}) was temporarily moved to {{ill|lt=Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463|WD=Q11665463}}.Kaneko (1983): p. 214 During the {{ill|lt=Pacific War|Q184425|WD=Q184425}}, the {{ill|lt=Ujiyamada air raid|Q18990749|WD=Q18990749}} occurred on July 29, 1945 (Shōwa 20). Although all surrounding houses burned down, due to desperate firefighting by the {{ill|lt=military|Q8473|WD=Q8473}} and the fact that an incendiary bomb lodged in the thatched roof failed to explode, only the shrine buildings of Tsukiyomi-no-miya remained standing amid the ruins.Yano (2006): pp. 184–185 However, a contracted shukueiin (guard attendant) was killed in the air raid, and the miyatsukasa (shrine official) suffered severe burns.Yano (2006): p. 185 === Festivals === Rites comparable to those of the Inner Shrine are performed, and for the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, Kannamesai, and Niinamesai, offerings ({{ill|lt=heihaku|Q11481885|WD=Q11481885}}) are presented from the {{ill|lt=Imperial Household|Q909452|WD=Q909452}}. * January ** Saitansai (New Year’s Day Festival) (January 1) A festival celebrating the New Year and praying for the eternal continuity of the imperial line. ** Genshisai (January 3) A festival celebrating the origin of the imperial succession at the start of the year. * February ** Kenkoku Kinen-sai (National Foundation Festival) (February 11) A festival celebrating the founding of the nation by {{ill|lt=Emperor Jimmu|Q200188|WD=Q200188}}. ** Kinensai (February 18) A festival held at the beginning of the year praying for abundant harvests and national peace. ** Tenchōsai (February 23) A festival celebrating the birthday of {{ill||lt=Emperor Naruhito|UNKNOWN}}. * May ** Kazahinomisai (May 14) A rite in which offerings are presented not only at the Outer and Inner Shrines but also at betsugu, massha, and sessha, praying that there will be no damage from wind and rain and that the five grains will be abundant. * June ** Tsukinamisai (June 18–19) A festival held in June and December on the 11th, praying for national peace and the emperor’s well-being; at the Shrine it is also called one of the “Three Seasonal Festivals” together with the Kannamesai. * August ** Kazahinomisai (August 4) Same as above. * October ** {{ill|lt=Kannamesai|Q11255045|WD=Q11255045}} (October 18–19) A festival in which priests offer newly harvested grain as sacred food ({{ill|lt=shinsen|Q11591045|WD=Q11591045|lt=Ōmike}}). * November ** {{ill|lt=Niinamesai|Q11501518|WD=Q11501518}} (November 24) A festival in which the emperor offers newly harvested grain to the gods, partakes of it himself, and gives thanks for the harvest. * December ** Tsukinamisai (December 18–19) === Shikinen sengū === [[File:Sengu of Tsukiyomi no Miya, August 2014.jpg|thumb|Tsukiyomi-no-miya before the Ritchūsai (photo taken August 11, 2014)
Left: the then-current shrine building; right: the shrine building under construction]] The ceremonies and schedule for the 62nd shikinen sengū of Tsukiyomi-no-miya are as follows:{{Cite web|ja|url=http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|title=Another “moon deity” of Ise Grand Shrine’s Outer Shrine betsugu also moves—only Kaze-no-miya remains|publisher=Ise-Shima Keizai Shimbun|date=2015-03-03|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307142246/http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|archivedate=2015-03-07}}{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|title=Relocations of 12 betsugu including Tsukiyomi-no-miya - Ise Grand Shrine|publisher=Jingu Administration Office|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210061619/http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|archivedate=2015-02-10}} **2014** * August 20 – Ritchūsai (Pillar-Raising Festival) / Jōtōsai (Ridgepole-Raising Festival) * October 5 – Nokitsukesai (Eaves-Attaching Festival) * November 5 – Irakasai (Roofing Festival) **2015** * February 26 – Mitosai / Mifunashiro Hōnōshiki / Araikiyome * February 27 – Kotsukisai / Gochinsai / Kawara Ōharae * February 28 – Okazari / Sengyo (Transfer of the deity) * March 1 – Ōmike / Hōhei Among these, the Ritchūsai, Jōtōsai, Kotsukisai, Gochinsai, Sengyo, and Hōhei are conducted according to dates determined by imperial decision. In addition, on February 22, 2015, the **Oshiraishi-mochi** event was held, in which about 1,000 people of the Miyago offering group pulled ceremonial carts loaded with sacred white stones for 1.2 km from the Uraguchi intersection to Tsukiyomi-no-miya.{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|title=“Enya” linking to the next generation: Oshiraishi-mochi event at Tsukiyomi-no-miya in Ise|author=Yudai Nakahira|publisher=Chunichi Shimbun|date=2015-02-23|accessdate=2015-03-08|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307161058/http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|archivedate=2015-03-07}} With this, all oshiraishi-mochi events for the betsugu were completed. === Precincts === * Tsukiyomi-no-miya — A betsugu of the Outer Shrine (Gekū) of the Ise Grand Shrine complex. In keeping with the Outer Shrine, the thatched **shinmei-zukuri** building faces south and has outward-cut chigi and five (an odd number) katsuogi. The old site for relocation (kodenchi) lies adjacent to it east–west. As with the Outer Shrine, a relocation ({{ill|lt=Shikinen sengū|Q3959472|WD=Q3959472}}) is performed once every 20 years. There is a tradition that when people of Miyago pulled the “yakukan” (construction timber) and reached Yōkaichiba-chō, a fire broke out in Miyago, and the pullers returned to fight it; the people of Yōkaichiba-chō took over pulling the timber, and ever since, at the **{{ill|lt=Okihiki-zome-shiki|Q11489125|WD=Q11489125}}** the people of Yōkaichiba-chō have pulled and offered the timber to Tsukiyomi-no-miya. * {{ill|lt=Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931|WD=Q17225931}} — Enshrined deity: the mitama (spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto. Located within the precincts of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, but it is a sessha of Toyouke Daijingu (the Outer Shrine) of Ise Grand Shrine. * {{ill||lt=Inari Shrine|UNKNOWN}} * Shukueiya === Kamiji Street === [[File:Kamiji Street from Tsukiyomi no Miya.jpg|thumb|Kamiji Street]] The straight road about 4 m wide running from the Outer Shrine’s Kita-mikado (North Gate) to Tsukiyomi-no-miya is regarded as “the road the gods pass,” and is called **Kamiji Street** (神路通り). See the article {{ill|lt=Kamiji Street|Q30114580|WD=Q30114580}}. === Devotee organization === In 1960 (Shōwa 35), a Tsukiyomi confraternity (Tsukiyomi-kō) was formed mainly by worshippers living in Ise, later renamed the Tsukiyomi-no-miya Hōsankai. The Hōsankai carries out activities such as holding a festival of gratitude for divine blessings on April 19 and September 19 each year. === Access === * About a 10-minute walk from {{ill|lt=Ise-shi Station|Q6079748|WD=Q6079748}} on the JR {{ill|lt=Sangū Line|Q872023|WD=Q872023}} and the Kintetsu Yamada Line. * About a 5-minute walk from the Outer Shrine Kita-mikado entrance via {{ill|lt=Kamiji Street|Q30114580|WD=Q30114580}}.JTB Publishing (2011): p. 43 * About a 3-minute walk from the Shindō bus stop (Mie Kōtsū), and immediately from the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop on the Ise City community bus “Okage Bus.”From July 20, 2013, Mie Kōtsū’s “Sangū Bus” stopped at the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop, but as of March 31, 2015, service to that stop was discontinued. * About 3 km from the Ise Interchange on the {{ill|lt=Ise Expressway|Q6079578|WD=Q6079578}}. * Parking: Only 2–4 cars can park in front of the torii gate, but there are parking meters on the road to the south. === It is a betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of the Outer Shrine (Gekū), {{ill|lt=Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343|WD=Q11633343}}, of the {{ill|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168|WD=Q687168}} complex.Tatsumi Publishing (2013): p. 16Ise Bunkasha, ed. (2008): p. 39Mirai Publishing (2013): p. 64Gakken Publishing (2013): p. 69JTB Publishing (2011): p. 42Publishing Business Headquarters, Domestic Information Dept., Third Editorial Dept., ed. (2014): p. 34Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 124 It is also a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|UNKNOWN}}. === Enshrined deities === {{ill|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520|lt=**Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**}} (つきよみのみこと) **{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto|UNKNOWN}}** (つきよみのみことのあらみたま) :Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto is the same deity as Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, who is enshrined at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine (Naikū). He is also said to be the younger brother of {{ill|lt=Amaterasu|Q455602|WD=Q455602}}. Because people historically planned farm work using a lunar calendar ({{ill|lt=lunar calendar|Q185688|WD=Q185688}}) based on the waxing and waning of the moon, he has been regarded as a deity connected with agriculture. He is also considered a river deity of Takagawara and a deity connected with women as well. In *Shinmei Hisho*, the sacred object ({{ill|lt=shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532}}) is described as a {{ill|lt=mirror|Q35197|WD=Q35197}}. === Overview === [[File:Tsukiyomi-nomiya(Geku)_00.JPG|thumb|300px|right|Tsukiyomi-no-miya seen from above]] Tsukiyomi-no-miya is a betsugu of the Outer Shrine located about 300 m north of the Gekū and about 500 m west of {{ill|lt=Ise-shi Station|Q6079748|WD=Q6079748}}. Two deities—{{ill|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520|lt=Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}} and his aramitama (rough/active spirit), **Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**—are enshrined together in the same shrine building. At Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and his aramitama are enshrined in separate buildings, but at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月夜見宮) they are enshrined together, which is a distinguishing feature. Other betsugu that enshrine two deities in a single building include {{ill|lt=Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463|WD=Q11665463}} (an Outer Shrine betsugu) and {{ill|lt=Kaza-hi-no-miya|Q11665488|WD=Q11665488}} (an Inner Shrine betsugu), both of which enshrine Shinatsuhiko-no-Mikoto and Shinatobe-no-Mikoto. Among the Outer Shrine’s betsugu, this is the only shrine located outside the main sacred precinct (miyagi). Although it stands in the urban area of Ise, the grounds retain a quiet atmosphere. The moat surrounding three sides of the precinct is thought to be a remnant of a tributary of the {{ill|lt=Miyagawa River (Mie)|Q6884164|WD=Q6884164}}. {{ill|lt=Mie Prefectural Route 37 (Toba–Matsusaka Line)|Q11357923|WD=Q11357923}}, which runs along the north side of the moat, becomes the venue for **{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hatsuhiki|UNKNOWN}}** (the “Oise Grand Festival”) held each October in conjunction with the {{ill|lt=Kannamesai|Q11255045|WD=Q11255045}}, and the ceremonial carts carrying first fruits into the Outer Shrine pass through. The Outer Shrine’s sessha (subsidiary shrine), **{{ill|lt=Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931|WD=Q17225931}}**, is located behind the right side of the main shrine building. Behind the left side, an {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Inari|UNKNOWN}} is enshrined. To the right stands a large camphor tree, where some visitors offer prayers. As with other outlying betsugu, there is a **shukueiya** (a station where shrine staff stay during visiting hours), which distributes amulets and talismans and arranges kagura performances and offerings. === History === Its origins are not certain, but it is said that in ancient times it was called **Takagawara** and was a shrine that enshrined an agricultural deity. In the *Engishiki* compiled in 927 (the 5th year of Engi) during the reign of the 60th emperor, {{ill|lt=Emperor Daigo|Q329753|WD=Q329753}}, it was ranked first among the Outer Shrine’s sessha. In the *Toyuke-no-miya Gishikichō* it is recorded as “Tsukuyomi Shrine,” in the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō* as “Tsukiyomi Shrine,” and in the *Ise Daijingū Shiki* as “Tsukiyomi Sha.” In 1210 (the 4th year of Jōgen), it was elevated to the status of a betsugu.Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 125 In the Meiji period, the Outer Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月夜見宮**, while the Inner Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月讀宮**. During the {{ill|lt=Ise riot|Q11379085|WD=Q11379085}} of 1876 (Meiji 9), nearby towns burned, and because of concern that the fire might spread to Tsukiyomi-no-miya, the sacred object ({{ill|lt=shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532}}) was temporarily moved to {{ill|lt=Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463|WD=Q11665463}}.Kaneko (1983): p. 214 During the {{ill|lt=Pacific War|Q184425|WD=Q184425}}, the {{ill|lt=Ujiyamada air raid|Q18990749|WD=Q18990749}} occurred on July 29, 1945 (Shōwa 20). Although all surrounding houses burned down, due to desperate firefighting by the {{ill|lt=military|Q8473|WD=Q8473}} and the fact that an incendiary bomb lodged in the thatched roof failed to explode, only the shrine buildings of Tsukiyomi-no-miya remained standing amid the ruins.Yano (2006): pp. 184–185 However, a contracted shukueiin (guard attendant) was killed in the air raid, and the miyatsukasa (shrine official) suffered severe burns.Yano (2006): p. 185 === Festivals === Rites comparable to those of the Inner Shrine are performed, and for the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, Kannamesai, and Niinamesai, offerings ({{ill|lt=heihaku|Q11481885|WD=Q11481885}}) are presented from the {{ill|lt=Imperial Household|Q909452|WD=Q909452}}. * January ** Saitansai (New Year’s Day Festival) (January 1) A festival celebrating the New Year and praying for the eternal continuity of the imperial line. ** Genshisai (January 3) A festival celebrating the origin of the imperial succession at the start of the year. * February ** Kenkoku Kinen-sai (National Foundation Festival) (February 11) A festival celebrating the founding of the nation by {{ill|lt=Emperor Jimmu|Q200188|WD=Q200188}}. ** Kinensai (February 18) A festival held at the beginning of the year praying for abundant harvests and national peace. ** Tenchōsai (February 23) A festival celebrating the birthday of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Emperor Naruhito|UNKNOWN}}. * May ** Kazahinomisai (May 14) A rite in which offerings are presented not only at the Outer and Inner Shrines but also at betsugu, massha, and sessha, praying that there will be no damage from wind and rain and that the five grains will be abundant. * June ** Tsukinamisai (June 18–19) A festival held in June and December on the 11th, praying for national peace and the emperor’s well-being; at the Shrine it is also called one of the “Three Seasonal Festivals” together with the Kannamesai. * August ** Kazahinomisai (August 4) Same as above. * October ** {{ill|lt=Kannamesai|Q11255045|WD=Q11255045}} (October 18–19) A festival in which priests offer newly harvested grain as sacred food ({{ill|lt=shinsen|Q11591045|WD=Q11591045|lt=Ōmike}}). * November ** {{ill|lt=Niinamesai|Q11501518|WD=Q11501518}} (November 24) A festival in which the emperor offers newly harvested grain to the gods, partakes of it himself, and gives thanks for the harvest. * December ** Tsukinamisai (December 18–19) === Shikinen sengū === [[File:Sengu of Tsukiyomi no Miya, August 2014.jpg|thumb|Tsukiyomi-no-miya before the Ritchūsai (photo taken August 11, 2014)
Left: the then-current shrine building; right: the shrine building under construction]] The ceremonies and schedule for the 62nd shikinen sengū of Tsukiyomi-no-miya are as follows:{{Cite web|ja|url=http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|title=Another “moon deity” of Ise Grand Shrine’s Outer Shrine betsugu also moves—only Kaze-no-miya remains|publisher=Ise-Shima Keizai Shimbun|date=2015-03-03|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307142246/http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|archivedate=2015-03-07}}{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|title=Relocations of 12 betsugu including Tsukiyomi-no-miya - Ise Grand Shrine|publisher=Jingu Administration Office|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210061619/http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|archivedate=2015-02-10}} **2014** * August 20 – Ritchūsai (Pillar-Raising Festival) / Jōtōsai (Ridgepole-Raising Festival) * October 5 – Nokitsukesai (Eaves-Attaching Festival) * November 5 – Irakasai (Roofing Festival) **2015** * February 26 – Mitosai / Mifunashiro Hōnōshiki / Araikiyome * February 27 – Kotsukisai / Gochinsai / Kawara Ōharae * February 28 – Okazari / Sengyo (Transfer of the deity) * March 1 – Ōmike / Hōhei Among these, the Ritchūsai, Jōtōsai, Kotsukisai, Gochinsai, Sengyo, and Hōhei are conducted according to dates determined by imperial decision. In addition, on February 22, 2015, the **Oshiraishi-mochi** event was held, in which about 1,000 people of the Miyago offering group pulled ceremonial carts loaded with sacred white stones for 1.2 km from the Uraguchi intersection to Tsukiyomi-no-miya.{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|title=“Enya” linking to the next generation: Oshiraishi-mochi event at Tsukiyomi-no-miya in Ise|author=Yudai Nakahira|publisher=Chunichi Shimbun|date=2015-02-23|accessdate=2015-03-08|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307161058/http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|archivedate=2015-03-07}} With this, all oshiraishi-mochi events for the betsugu were completed. === Precincts === * Tsukiyomi-no-miya — A betsugu of the Outer Shrine (Gekū) of the Ise Grand Shrine complex. In keeping with the Outer Shrine, the thatched **shinmei-zukuri** building faces south and has outward-cut chigi and five (an odd number) katsuogi. The old site for relocation (kodenchi) lies adjacent to it east–west. As with the Outer Shrine, a relocation ({{ill|lt=Shikinen sengū|Q3959472|WD=Q3959472}}) is performed once every 20 years. There is a tradition that when people of Miyago pulled the “yakukan” (construction timber) and reached Yōkaichiba-chō, a fire broke out in Miyago, and the pullers returned to fight it; the people of Yōkaichiba-chō took over pulling the timber, and ever since, at the **{{ill|lt=Okihiki-zome-shiki|Q11489125|WD=Q11489125}}** the people of Yōkaichiba-chō have pulled and offered the timber to Tsukiyomi-no-miya. * {{ill|lt=Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931|WD=Q17225931}} — Enshrined deity: the mitama (spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto. Located within the precincts of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, but it is a sessha of Toyouke Daijingu (the Outer Shrine) of Ise Grand Shrine. * {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Inari Shrine|UNKNOWN}} * Shukueiya === Kamiji Street === [[File:Kamiji Street from Tsukiyomi no Miya.jpg|thumb|Kamiji Street]] The straight road about 4 m wide running from the Outer Shrine’s Kita-mikado (North Gate) to Tsukiyomi-no-miya is regarded as “the road the gods pass,” and is called **Kamiji Street** (神路通り). See the article {{ill|lt=Kamiji Street|Q30114580|WD=Q30114580}}. === Devotee organization === In 1960 (Shōwa 35), a Tsukiyomi confraternity (Tsukiyomi-kō) was formed mainly by worshippers living in Ise, later renamed the Tsukiyomi-no-miya Hōsankai. The Hōsankai carries out activities such as holding a festival of gratitude for divine blessings on April 19 and September 19 each year. === Access === * About a 10-minute walk from {{ill|lt=Ise-shi Station|Q6079748|WD=Q6079748}} on the JR {{ill|lt=Sangū Line|Q872023|WD=Q872023}} and the Kintetsu Yamada Line. * About a 5-minute walk from the Outer Shrine Kita-mikado entrance via {{ill|lt=Kamiji Street|Q30114580|WD=Q30114580}}.JTB Publishing (2011): p. 43 * About a 3-minute walk from the Shindō bus stop (Mie Kōtsū), and immediately from the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop on the Ise City community bus “Okage Bus.”From July 20, 2013, Mie Kōtsū’s “Sangū Bus” stopped at the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop, but as of March 31, 2015, service to that stop was discontinued. * About 3 km from the Ise Interchange on the {{ill|lt=Ise Expressway|Q6079578|WD=Q6079578}}. * Parking: Only 2–4 cars can park in front of the torii gate, but there are parking meters on the road to the south. === It is a betsugu (auxiliary shrine) of the Outer Shrine (Gekū), {{ill|lt=Toyouke Daijingu|Q11633343|WD=Q11633343}}, of the {{ill|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168|WD=Q687168}} complex.Tatsumi Publishing (2013): p. 16Ise Bunkasha, ed. (2008): p. 39Mirai Publishing (2013): p. 64Gakken Publishing (2013): p. 69JTB Publishing (2011): p. 42Publishing Business Headquarters, Domestic Information Dept., Third Editorial Dept., ed. (2014): p. 34Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 124 It is also a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}}. === Enshrined deities === {{ill|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520|lt=**Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**}} (つきよみのみこと) **{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}}** (つきよみのみことのあらみたま) :Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto is the same deity as Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, who is enshrined at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine (Naikū). He is also said to be the younger brother of {{ill|lt=Amaterasu|Q455602|WD=Q455602}}. Because people historically planned farm work using a lunar calendar ({{ill|lt=lunar calendar|Q185688|WD=Q185688}}) based on the waxing and waning of the moon, he has been regarded as a deity connected with agriculture. He is also considered a river deity of Takagawara and a deity connected with women as well. In *Shinmei Hisho*, the sacred object ({{ill|lt=shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532}}) is described as a {{ill|lt=mirror|Q35197|WD=Q35197}}. === Overview === [[File:Tsukiyomi-nomiya(Geku)_00.JPG|thumb|300px|right|Tsukiyomi-no-miya seen from above]] Tsukiyomi-no-miya is a betsugu of the Outer Shrine located about 300 m north of the Gekū and about 500 m west of {{ill|lt=Ise-shi Station|Q6079748|WD=Q6079748}}. Two deities—{{ill|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520|lt=Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto}} and his aramitama (rough/active spirit), **Aramitama of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto**—are enshrined together in the same shrine building. At Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月讀宮), a betsugu of the Inner Shrine, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and his aramitama are enshrined in separate buildings, but at Tsukiyomi-no-miya (月夜見宮) they are enshrined together, which is a distinguishing feature. Other betsugu that enshrine two deities in a single building include {{ill|lt=Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463|WD=Q11665463}} (an Outer Shrine betsugu) and {{ill|lt=Kaza-hi-no-miya|Q11665488|WD=Q11665488}} (an Inner Shrine betsugu), both of which enshrine Shinatsuhiko-no-Mikoto and Shinatobe-no-Mikoto. Among the Outer Shrine’s betsugu, this is the only shrine located outside the main sacred precinct (miyagi). Although it stands in the urban area of Ise, the grounds retain a quiet atmosphere. The moat surrounding three sides of the precinct is thought to be a remnant of a tributary of the {{ill|lt=Miyagawa River (Mie)|Q6884164|WD=Q6884164}}. {{ill|lt=Mie Prefectural Route 37 (Toba–Matsusaka Line)|Q11357923|WD=Q11357923}}, which runs along the north side of the moat, becomes the venue for **{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hatsuhiki|1=UNKNOWN}}** (the “Oise Grand Festival”) held each October in conjunction with the {{ill|lt=Kannamesai|Q11255045|WD=Q11255045}}, and the ceremonial carts carrying first fruits into the Outer Shrine pass through. The Outer Shrine’s sessha (subsidiary shrine), **{{ill|lt=Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931|WD=Q17225931}}**, is located behind the right side of the main shrine building. Behind the left side, an {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Inari|1=UNKNOWN}} is enshrined. To the right stands a large camphor tree, where some visitors offer prayers. As with other outlying betsugu, there is a **shukueiya** (a station where shrine staff stay during visiting hours), which distributes amulets and talismans and arranges kagura performances and offerings. === History === Its origins are not certain, but it is said that in ancient times it was called **Takagawara** and was a shrine that enshrined an agricultural deity. In the *Engishiki* compiled in 927 (the 5th year of Engi) during the reign of the 60th emperor, {{ill|lt=Emperor Daigo|Q329753|WD=Q329753}}, it was ranked first among the Outer Shrine’s sessha. In the *Toyuke-no-miya Gishikichō* it is recorded as “Tsukuyomi Shrine,” in the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō* as “Tsukiyomi Shrine,” and in the *Ise Daijingū Shiki* as “Tsukiyomi Sha.” In 1210 (the 4th year of Jōgen), it was elevated to the status of a betsugu.Mitsuhashi (2013): p. 125 In the Meiji period, the Outer Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月夜見宮**, while the Inner Shrine betsugu “tsukiyomi-no-miya” came to be written as **月讀宮**. During the {{ill|lt=Ise riot|Q11379085|WD=Q11379085}} of 1876 (Meiji 9), nearby towns burned, and because of concern that the fire might spread to Tsukiyomi-no-miya, the sacred object ({{ill|lt=shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532}}) was temporarily moved to {{ill|lt=Kaze-no-miya|Q11665463|WD=Q11665463}}.Kaneko (1983): p. 214 During the {{ill|lt=Pacific War|Q184425|WD=Q184425}}, the {{ill|lt=Ujiyamada air raid|Q18990749|WD=Q18990749}} occurred on July 29, 1945 (Shōwa 20). Although all surrounding houses burned down, due to desperate firefighting by the {{ill|lt=military|Q8473|WD=Q8473}} and the fact that an incendiary bomb lodged in the thatched roof failed to explode, only the shrine buildings of Tsukiyomi-no-miya remained standing amid the ruins.Yano (2006): pp. 184–185 However, a contracted shukueiin (guard attendant) was killed in the air raid, and the miyatsukasa (shrine official) suffered severe burns.Yano (2006): p. 185 === Festivals === Rites comparable to those of the Inner Shrine are performed, and for the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, Kannamesai, and Niinamesai, offerings ({{ill|lt=heihaku|Q11481885|WD=Q11481885}}) are presented from the {{ill|lt=Imperial Household|Q909452|WD=Q909452}}. * January ** Saitansai (New Year’s Day Festival) (January 1) A festival celebrating the New Year and praying for the eternal continuity of the imperial line. ** Genshisai (January 3) A festival celebrating the origin of the imperial succession at the start of the year. * February ** Kenkoku Kinen-sai (National Foundation Festival) (February 11) A festival celebrating the founding of the nation by {{ill|lt=Emperor Jimmu|Q200188|WD=Q200188}}. ** Kinensai (February 18) A festival held at the beginning of the year praying for abundant harvests and national peace. ** Tenchōsai (February 23) A festival celebrating the birthday of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Emperor Naruhito|1=UNKNOWN}}. * May ** Kazahinomisai (May 14) A rite in which offerings are presented not only at the Outer and Inner Shrines but also at betsugu, massha, and sessha, praying that there will be no damage from wind and rain and that the five grains will be abundant. * June ** Tsukinamisai (June 18–19) A festival held in June and December on the 11th, praying for national peace and the emperor’s well-being; at the Shrine it is also called one of the “Three Seasonal Festivals” together with the Kannamesai. * August ** Kazahinomisai (August 4) Same as above. * October ** {{ill|lt=Kannamesai|Q11255045|WD=Q11255045}} (October 18–19) A festival in which priests offer newly harvested grain as sacred food ({{ill|lt=shinsen|Q11591045|WD=Q11591045|lt=Ōmike}}). * November ** {{ill|lt=Niinamesai|Q11501518|WD=Q11501518}} (November 24) A festival in which the emperor offers newly harvested grain to the gods, partakes of it himself, and gives thanks for the harvest. * December ** Tsukinamisai (December 18–19) === Shikinen sengū === [[File:Sengu of Tsukiyomi no Miya, August 2014.jpg|thumb|Tsukiyomi-no-miya before the Ritchūsai (photo taken August 11, 2014)
Left: the then-current shrine building; right: the shrine building under construction]] The ceremonies and schedule for the 62nd shikinen sengū of Tsukiyomi-no-miya are as follows:{{Cite web|ja|url=http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|title=Another “moon deity” of Ise Grand Shrine’s Outer Shrine betsugu also moves—only Kaze-no-miya remains|publisher=Ise-Shima Keizai Shimbun|date=2015-03-03|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307142246/http://iseshima.keizai.biz/headline/2259/|archivedate=2015-03-07}}{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|title=Relocations of 12 betsugu including Tsukiyomi-no-miya - Ise Grand Shrine|publisher=Jingu Administration Office|accessdate=2015-03-07|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210061619/http://www.isejingu.or.jp/sikinen_2.html|archivedate=2015-02-10}} **2014** * August 20 – Ritchūsai (Pillar-Raising Festival) / Jōtōsai (Ridgepole-Raising Festival) * October 5 – Nokitsukesai (Eaves-Attaching Festival) * November 5 – Irakasai (Roofing Festival) **2015** * February 26 – Mitosai / Mifunashiro Hōnōshiki / Araikiyome * February 27 – Kotsukisai / Gochinsai / Kawara Ōharae * February 28 – Okazari / Sengyo (Transfer of the deity) * March 1 – Ōmike / Hōhei Among these, the Ritchūsai, Jōtōsai, Kotsukisai, Gochinsai, Sengyo, and Hōhei are conducted according to dates determined by imperial decision. In addition, on February 22, 2015, the **Oshiraishi-mochi** event was held, in which about 1,000 people of the Miyago offering group pulled ceremonial carts loaded with sacred white stones for 1.2 km from the Uraguchi intersection to Tsukiyomi-no-miya.{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|title=“Enya” linking to the next generation: Oshiraishi-mochi event at Tsukiyomi-no-miya in Ise|author=Yudai Nakahira|publisher=Chunichi Shimbun|date=2015-02-23|accessdate=2015-03-08|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150307161058/http://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/mie/20150223/CK2015022302000028.html|archivedate=2015-03-07}} With this, all oshiraishi-mochi events for the betsugu were completed. === Precincts === * Tsukiyomi-no-miya — A betsugu of the Outer Shrine (Gekū) of the Ise Grand Shrine complex. In keeping with the Outer Shrine, the thatched **shinmei-zukuri** building faces south and has outward-cut chigi and five (an odd number) katsuogi. The old site for relocation (kodenchi) lies adjacent to it east–west. As with the Outer Shrine, a relocation ({{ill|lt=Shikinen sengū|Q3959472|WD=Q3959472}}) is performed once every 20 years. There is a tradition that when people of Miyago pulled the “yakukan” (construction timber) and reached Yōkaichiba-chō, a fire broke out in Miyago, and the pullers returned to fight it; the people of Yōkaichiba-chō took over pulling the timber, and ever since, at the **{{ill|lt=Okihiki-zome-shiki|Q11489125|WD=Q11489125}}** the people of Yōkaichiba-chō have pulled and offered the timber to Tsukiyomi-no-miya. * {{ill|lt=Takagawara Shrine|Q17225931|WD=Q17225931}} — Enshrined deity: the mitama (spirit) of Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto. Located within the precincts of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, but it is a sessha of Toyouke Daijingu (the Outer Shrine) of Ise Grand Shrine. * {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Inari Shrine|1=UNKNOWN}} * Shukueiya === Kamiji Street === [[File:Kamiji Street from Tsukiyomi no Miya.jpg|thumb|Kamiji Street]] The straight road about 4 m wide running from the Outer Shrine’s Kita-mikado (North Gate) to Tsukiyomi-no-miya is regarded as “the road the gods pass,” and is called **Kamiji Street** (神路通り). See the article {{ill|lt=Kamiji Street|Q30114580|WD=Q30114580}}. === Devotee organization === In 1960 (Shōwa 35), a Tsukiyomi confraternity (Tsukiyomi-kō) was formed mainly by worshippers living in Ise, later renamed the Tsukiyomi-no-miya Hōsankai. The Hōsankai carries out activities such as holding a festival of gratitude for divine blessings on April 19 and September 19 each year. === Access === * About a 10-minute walk from {{ill|lt=Ise-shi Station|Q6079748|WD=Q6079748}} on the JR {{ill|lt=Sangū Line|Q872023|WD=Q872023}} and the Kintetsu Yamada Line. * About a 5-minute walk from the Outer Shrine Kita-mikado entrance via {{ill|lt=Kamiji Street|Q30114580|WD=Q30114580}}.JTB Publishing (2011): p. 43 * About a 3-minute walk from the Shindō bus stop (Mie Kōtsū), and immediately from the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop on the Ise City community bus “Okage Bus.”From July 20, 2013, Mie Kōtsū’s “Sangū Bus” stopped at the “Tsukiyomi-no-miya-mae” stop, but as of March 31, 2015, service to that stop was discontinued. * About 3 km from the Ise Interchange on the {{ill|lt=Ise Expressway|Q6079578|WD=Q6079578}}. * Parking: Only 2–4 cars can park in front of the torii gate, but there are parking meters on the road to the south. === Ise Jingu Pilgrimage Perfect Book*, Mirai Publishing, Dec. 10, 2013, 107 pp. ISBN 978-4-907292-14-0 === See also === * {{ill|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520}} * {{ill|lt=List of Shikinaisha in Ise Province|Q11378973|WD=Q11378973}} * {{ill|lt=List of 125 shrines of Jingu|Q16482760|WD=Q16482760}} * {{ill|lt=Kamiji Street|Q30114580|WD=Q30114580}} === External links === {{commonscat|Tsukiyomi-no-miya (Geku)}} * {{Wayback|url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/about/geku/tsukiyomi.html |title=Tsukiyomi-no-miya |date=20170602200335}} - Official Ise Grand Shrine website * [http://www.jingukaikan.jp/125mairi/m02/0202.html Tsukiyomi-no-miya (つきよみのみや) - Jingu Kaikan] - Ise Jingu Sūkeikai (General Incorporated Foundation) * [http://www.ise-kanko.jp/base_data/base_data.php?info_cd=00269 Ise City Tourism Association / Tsukiyomi-no-miya] * [http://www.barifuri.com/tourcenter/data_kankou/tsukiyomi_1/index.html Tsukiyomi-no-miya (つきよみのみや)] - Ise-Shima Barrier-Free Tour Center {{Jingu 125 Shrines}} {{Shinto}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Tsukiyomi-no-miya}} == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Tsukiyomi-no-Miya (Geku)]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Tsukiyomi-no-Miya (Geku)]][[Category:pages]][[Category:pages]] [[Category:Shikinai Shōsha]] [[Category:Shikinai Hiteisha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Ise Province]] [[Category:pages]] [[Category:神宮125社]] [[Category:伊勢国の式内社]] [[Category:伊勢市の神社]] [[Category:2015年竣工の日本の建築物]]
